title: Ostia (9.10)
hookLine: mother and son rise in conversation to touch eternal wisdom for a moment
tomorrow: what was the one thing Monica asked for at the end?

cards: Late at night on a long drive, somebody in the passenger seat asks what happens after we die. Augustine and his mother, Monica, have that talk at a window in Ostia, a port by the Tiber, resting before a sea voyage.
They ask each other what the eternal life of the saints will be like. And while they talk, he says, they begin to rise.

teach.b: First, the climb. Step by step, he says, they go up through everything made: the earth, the sky, the sun, the moon and the stars, then into their own minds, and beyond.
Then, in his Latin: attingimus eam modice toto ictu cordis.
They touched wisdom itself, a little, with the whole beat of the heart. Then they sighed and came back down to the noise of speech, where words begin and end. For a moment, and then not.
Now the debate their question opens.
One view: heaven is, above all, seeing God. The Catechism calls it seeing God face to face, as he is. Everything else is secondary.
The other view: heaven is also each other. The same Catechism calls heaven a communion of life and love with the Trinity, with Mary, the angels and all the blessed.
A grandmother at a funeral saying we'll see them again isn't being sentimental; she's naming the communion of saints.
At Ostia, both views get a voice. What they touch is wisdom itself, beyond everything made. But they get there together, a mother and a son at a window, talking.

how: The Church honors Monica as a saint, and Catholics read the conversation at Ostia as a picture of contemplation: a brief foretaste of heaven, given in ordinary friendship and talk.

s: Augustine says he and Monica stayed in that vision for hours
for a moment: modice, a little. then they came back down to the noise of speech.
at Ostia they were talking about what the life of the saints would be like
that question is what they were asking each other when they began to rise.
the Church teaches heaven is only about God, with no one else there
the Catechism calls heaven a communion with the Trinity, Mary, the angels and all the blessed.

games.q: you lean toward "heaven is seeing God." your aunt says it's being with her late husband again. what's the strongest case for her side?
o: the Catechism calls heaven a communion with all the blessed.
people only say that at funerals to feel better.
Augustine never mentions anyone else in heaven.
games.why: the Catechism holds both: seeing God face to face, and a communion of life and love with all the blessed. At Ostia, a mother and son rise toward wisdom together.

practice: Think of one person you could ask what they hope heaven is like. Write the question as a text, in your own words, simple enough to send over breakfast. Send it or keep it, and spend the sit with how you'd answer it yourself.
